final_answer: TCP congestion control uses both slow start and congestion avoidance because they serve complementary purposes. Slow start exponentially increases the congestion window to quickly probe network capacity at the beginning of a connection, doubling cwnd each RTT while segments are successfully acknowledged. Congestion avoidance then increases the window linearly, incrementing cwnd by one segment per RTT once the slow start threshold is reached, to avoid inducing congestion. One algorithm for the slow start phase is the slow start algorithm itself, and one for congestion avoidance is the additive-increase congestion avoidance algorithm, both defined in RFC 5681.

final_answer: A hash table is a data structure used to insert, look up, and remove key-value pairs quickly, operating on the hashing concept where each key is translated by a hash function into an index in an array. Lookups are described as O(1) because a hash table is effectively an array with a map to the index: an array lookup is O(1) since memory is addressable, and the hash table adds the constant-time step of computing a bucket index before the array access. However, this is the average-case time complexity; worst case may require O(n) time where n is the number of elements in the table, typically when collisions occur. Maintaining O(1) depends on a good hash function, collision resolution techniques like chaining, open addressing, and double hashing, and dynamic resizing to keep an ideal load factor.

final_answer: Single-request transformer inference is memory-bandwidth bound because, for each generated token, the entire model weights must be loaded from VRAM and used in a full forward pass, so memory traffic from weights and the KV cache exceeds computation time; no-batch inference is well established as memory-bound. This reflects low arithmetic intensity in decode: relatively few floating-point operations are needed compared to loading the entire model weights, whereas high-intensity prefill is compute-bound on the same hardware. Because the bottleneck is bandwidth rather than compute, no compute optimization will make single-request decode faster; the standard mitigation is batching, which performs more compute for the same memory traffic.
key_points: For each generated token in single-request decode, the entire model weights must be loaded from VRAM and used in a full forward pass, so weight plus KV-cache memory traffic exceeds computation time.
Decode has low arithmetic intensity—few FLOPs relative to bytes of weights loaded—making it memory-bound, while high-intensity prefill is compute-bound on the same hardware.

Because bandwidth is the bottleneck, compute optimization cannot speed up single-request decode; batching more requests increases compute for the same memory traffic and shifts the workload away from being memory bound.
